Alpha
AL-fuh
n.
From Greek alpha (α), the first letter of the Greek alphabet; borrowed directly into Latin and English from Hellenistic usage. Derives ultimately from Phoenician aleph (“ox”), the pictographic ancestor of all alphabetic scripts. In classical rhetoric and logic, alpha was the natural symbol of beginning, primacy, and first-rank status.

Biblical Definition

In Scripture the letter alpha receives its supreme significance when the risen Christ claims it as a divine self-designation. “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is, and who was, and who is to come — the Almighty” (Rev 1:8). Alpha, as the first letter of the Greek alphabet, signifies absolute primacy — not chronological firstness among a sequence of things, but the original and uncaused Beginning in which all things have their source. In ancient letter-symbolism, alpha carried the weight of first-rank reality: what comes first in order determines everything that follows. Christ's claim to be the Alpha is therefore a claim to be the originating cause and constitutive principle of all creation. The Gospel of John captures the same reality without the alphabetic symbol: “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1:1) — the Logos who was pros ton Theon before anything existed. At Revelation 22:13 the Alpha title is compounded with three further pairs — “the First and the Last, the Beginning and the End” — making plain that these are not three metaphors for three things but one truth told three ways: absolute divine sovereignty over the entire span from initiation to consummation. Alpha means that nothing precedes Christ; nothing is prior to Him; nothing stands over Him as a cause or condition. All that exists derives its being from the One who is the Alpha — which is precisely why every knee will bow at His name (Phil 2:10) and why every created intelligence must render to Him the worship that belongs to the first and only underived Reality.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) records alpha as the first letter of the Greek alphabet, and notes its use as a symbol of priority, primacy, and beginning — carried into Scripture as a divine title for the One who is first in all things and from whom all things derive their being.

expand to see more

ALPHA, n. [Gr. α.] The first letter of the Greek alphabet, corresponding to the English A. Used figuratively by Webster to denote primacy, priority, and the highest rank — that which stands at the head of all things.

In theological application, alpha becomes a divine title only in the New Testament, specifically in the Revelation of John, where the risen Christ claims the full span from alpha to omega — first to last — as His own sovereign domain, identifying Himself with the God who spoke to Isaiah: “I am the first, and I am the last; and beside me there is no God” (Isa 44:6).

Key Scripture

Revelation 1:8 — "“I am the Alpha and the Omega,” says the Lord God, “who is, and who was, and who is to come — the Almighty.”"

Revelation 22:13 — "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end, the first and the last."

Revelation 21:6 — "And he said unto me, It is done. I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end. I will give unto him that is athirst of the fountain of the water of life freely."

John 8:58 — "Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am."

Modern Corruption

New Age spirituality conscripts the alpha symbol as mystical energy-language; academic Christology reduces the title to a cultural trope borrowed from Hellenistic emperor-cult rather than a claim to divine self-existence; “alpha” in popular culture has been secularized to mean dominant social status with no reference to the One who holds all primacy.

expand to see more

Hellenistic-backgrounds scholarship has long attempted to domesticate the Alpha title by situating it within emperor-cult rhetoric or Stoic cosmological language, as though the risen Christ were borrowing a cultural prestige-symbol rather than asserting His identity as the self-existent God of Israel. This reading neuters the title: instead of “I am the uncaused First,” it becomes “I am first among the great figures.” The grammar of Revelation will not permit this reduction. The Alpha who speaks in Rev 1:8 is identified immediately as “the Almighty” — the Pantokrator — the title Scripture reserves for God alone.

In secular and New Age usage, “alpha” has been captured as a symbol of masculine dominance, social hierarchy, or mystical energy. The “alpha male” of popular psychology has no connection to the divine self-designation of Rev 1:8. The New Age use of alpha brain-waves and alpha frequencies borrows the letter's symbolic primacy while severing it entirely from the personal God who coined the title. These are the twin corruptions: flattening the divine into human social competition, and dissolving the personal into cosmic force.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Alpha descends from Phoenician pictographic writing through Greek into every subsequent Western alphabet, carrying its first-letter status across three thousand years of literacy; Scripture uses this universal primacy-symbol to declare Christ's absolute priority over all created reality.

expand to see more

Phoenician aleph — pictographic “ox,” the first letter of the Semitic alphabet; ancestor of all Western letters.

Greek alpha (α) — first letter of the Greek alphabet; used in classical logic to mark the primary premise.

Latin alpha — borrowed directly from Greek; retained in ecclesiastical and academic Latin as a symbol of primacy.

English alpha — used as an adjective meaning “first-rank” or “primary” in scientific and social nomenclature.

Biblical Greek to alpha — as a divine title in Revelation, alpha is deployed not as an academic symbol but as a first-person divine claim: “I am the Alpha.”

Usage

"When Christ declares “I am the Alpha,” He is not simply claiming historical priority but ontological primacy — He is the One without whom nothing was made that was made, the Beginning in whom the creation has its very cause."

"The Alpha title in Rev 1:8 is paired with “who is, and who was, and who is to come” — the Johannine threefold rendering of the Tetragrammaton — confirming that the Alpha who speaks is Jehovah Himself, the self-existent God of Exodus 3:14."

"In patristic and Reformed exegesis, the Alpha-Omega title establishes that history is not open-ended or contingent: it has a Beginning who is God and an End who is God, and all that unfolds between belongs to Him."
